segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: English and Spanish are two related languages. English is considered a Germanic language, but it's it's kind of half Latin. We have a huge amount of Latin vocabulary in English.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And this Latin vocabulary, we can convert it over to Spanish really easily, because Spanish is practically modern Latin. Whoever said Latin is a dead language lied. Just in the same way that Greek is a modern version of Ancient Greek, Spanish is like a modern version of Latin. It's actually street Latin that became Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we can identify Latin words in English, and we can, with just some rule or other, convert them over to Spanish, and this will give us around 3,000 words. I didn't count them, but there are around 3,000 words.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, for example, one of these rules is that words ending in -al tend to come from Latin, so we can make them Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So to give you an example: "normal" in Spanish is "normal".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Normal. Good. What do you notice different between "normal" and "normal"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What do you mean by the accent?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Well, the, um... Well, where the sound is stressed, which which vowel is stressed.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Where is it stressed in English?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. At the beginning, right? Normal, normal. And in Spanish we stress the end, right? Normal, normal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Um, so if we assume the same happens with other words, how do you think you would say metal?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Metal. To get a perfect accent in Spanish, we just need to pronounce all of the vowels exactly as they are written. So a, e, i, o, u, in Spanish is a, e, i, o, u. Where in English, the vowel, it can have many different sounds. Like if you look at the A sound in apple or in mare, it's very different sound. But A in Spanish is always going to be /a/.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: E is always going to be /e/. So if we pronounce the vowels as they're written, not these kind of, you know, these "uh, uh, uh" English vowels that we get, then we get a perfect Spanish accent.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Perfect. So we can begin to make sentences with this already. The word for "is" in Spanish is "es" (e-s).

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Es. And this also means "it is", "she is", "he is", or even "you are" talking to somebody formally. So now we can say, "He is normal", "she is normal".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah. Es normal. And you pronounced an S, which is excellent. English speakers should beware that maybe they feel themselves pronouncing a Z, because many times we have an S in English like in the word "is" and we pronounce a Z. So you might find slipping out "ez", but this is incorrect. You should be careful to pronounce an S: es. Es normal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say legal? Legal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, legal. So how would you say, "It is legal"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ilegal. Good. So here in English, like we have an I and an E producing the same sound: i-l, illegal. The I and the E is producing the same sound, so this is really confusing if you want to learn English. But in Spanish you're not going to have these problems. The I is like in "ink", and the E is like in "elephant": ilegal, ilegal. So, "It is illegal"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es ilegal. What if you wanted to say, "He is liberal"? You not need the word for "he" if you know who you're talking about; you can just use "es".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah. Es liberal. Now, Spanish is much more phonetic than English. What that means is that the letters are going to represent the same sound, where English has a million rules and a million exceptions to those rules and, I mean, it's really hard even for native English speakers often to understand how to pronounce a new word when they see it written. But you're not going to have that problem in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you know "natural", and you don't just want to change the accent and say "natural". This is not Spanish. You want to think how is it written and pronounce the letters as they are. So how do you think you would say natural in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Natural. Good, that's a T, so you pronounce a T. A is like /a/, U is like /u/: natural. Very good. And the accent on the end as well. "It's natural"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Es natural. If you want to say, "It isn't" or "it's not", the word for "not" or "don't" is the same as the word for "no". And the word for "no" in Spanish is the same as the word for "no" in English, but you pronounce it like in Spanish. So how do you think you say no in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No, good. And you put this before "is" if you want to say, "It is not", "he is not", "she is not", "you (formal) are not". So how would that sound, "It is not"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No es. Good. So now we can say things like, "It's not normal".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No es normal. How would you say ideal? So really think about how it's spelled, and try and pronounce each of those vowels as they're written: I like "ink", E like "elephant", A like "apple".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Ideal. How would you say, "It's ideal"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No es ideal. Perfect. How would you say fatal?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mmm, so think about how it's written.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, and perfect Spanish accent, huh? Cultural. Very nice. Annual?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Anual. And you cut this Y sound that comes in English: an-yual, annual. This Y sound comes from nowhere in English, and you cut it out because you focused on how it's written: anual. Very nice. Dental?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Tooth" in Spanish is "diente". So this is coming from "dental". So if you look up tooth in the dictionary and you find "diente", rather than treating it as like a random piece of vocabulary that you have to memorize, you can relate it back to dental. "Ah, okay, like dental, it comes from there." And this is useful for for memory.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Verbal. So if we wanted to say verb, we might not have a rule to convert that word over, but if we know verbal is "verbal", we can guess that verb is probably going to be the same in Spanish. And most of the time words that are the same that we don't have a rule, maybe we need to stick an O or an E or an A on the end, so we can make a guess. How do you think you say verb in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah! That's right! So with structure, with the building when we going to be making sentences with these words, we don't ever want to guess. We want to take our time and think it through. But with vocabulary, we can happily guess and try. Imagine we said "verba", for example, and they would look at us funny and they would go, "Ah, verbo!" And when that person says, "Ah, verbo!" then we learn, "Oh, okay, this is the right word." And it's the best way to learn quickly.
